question.note: Generic 'stigmatizing language in political advertisements', but the quote ties it to this ad; perceptions (Q1) and representation (Q3).

flags.text: Says 'stigmatizing language in political ads' worsens perceptions. The paper tested one advertisement (mugshot plus the 'CONVICTED CRIMINAL' label) and says the image and wording cannot be disentangled (p.17); it does not show that the language itself, or political ads in general, have this effect.

central_claim.note: Gives the harm to perceptions and the counter-narrative's mitigation; omits the improvement in representation.

evidence.note: Survey experiment (E1 without Democrats, Prolific, dates or pre-registration) and N = 2,439 in three groups (E2 without the arms' names or counts in the claim).

flags.text: 'The counter-narrative increased positive perceptions' drops that it was shown before the ad and compared with the ad alone; there was no counter-narrative-only arm (p.16).

key_findings.note: Only quote is NOT IN PAPER: it recasts hypothesis H1B (p.6, 'will significantly increase') as a result. No credit.
Names the quality of Democratic representation; omits the increase in belief in public-service motives.

scope_and_limits.note: Restates the paper's list of limitation dimensions (p.16) and garbles it: the paper lists design/modality, external validity and measurement as separate dimensions. No specific limitation or consequence; no credit, no flag.

interlocutor_claim.note: Garbled wording, but it is the meta-analysis claim (ref 7, p.2).
